text: follow- on treatment with clindamycin.8-10 Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) or mefloquine may be given as alternatives where first-line treatment is not tolerated or no other treat- ment options are available.10 Although fetal abnormalities have been associated with the use of high doses of chloro- quine, extensive clinical experience suggests it is safe; its value is limited, however, due to resistance. The CDC rec- ommends oral chloroquine for pregnant women with ma- laria infections acquired in chloroquine-sensitive areas and with non-falciparum malaria, although chloroquine-resist- ant P. vivax should be treated with quinine.10 Radical cure for patients with vivax or ovale malaria during pregnancy should be postponed until after delivery due to the risk of intravascular haemolysis in the mother and fetus;10,12 weekly chloroquine can be given during the remaining weeks of pregnancy. WHO recommends chloroquine or amodiaquine for pregnant women with P. vivax malaria.2 There may be difficulty if other drugs are required as opin- ion varies over their suitability. The tetracyclines are con- tra-indicated due to adverse effects on bone growth and teeth. Treatment of splenomegaly syndrome. A few individu- als infected with Plasmodium develop chronic hyperreac- tive malarial splenomegaly syndrome, an aberrant immu- nological response formerly known as the tropical splenomegaly syndrome. Traditionally, patients have first received a full course of antimalarial chemotherapy appro- priate to the causative species followed by lengthy and probably lifelong chemoprophylaxis; however, a study in 312 patients suggested that pyrimethamine given with fo- linic acid for 30 days could produce a rapid reduction of splenomegaly which persisted for at least 3 months.13 PROPHYLAXIS OF MALARIA Chemoprophylaxis of malaria may refer to absolute pre- vention of infection (causal prophylaxis) or to suppression of parasitaemia and its symptoms (clinical prophylaxis). Causal prophylaxis is provided by tissue schizontocides which destroy the exoerythrocytic forms of the parasite. Clinical prophylaxis is provided by blood schizontocides which, if continued until all exoerythrocytic forms of the parasite are destroyed, will ultimately produce a suppres- sive cure. In P. falciparum infections this would be achieved by about a month after the last infected bite, but relapses with P. vivax and P. ovale may still occur after standard clinical prophylactic regimens due to the pres- ence of latent exoerythrocytic forms (hypnozoites).
